adjustments.before: Ideen om, hvordan jeg kunne lære at skrive, kom til mig ved at være i Durgin og Baileys skibsværft, hvor jeg ofte så skibstømrerne, efter at have tilhugget et stykke tømmer og gjort det klar til brug, skrive på det navnet på den del af skibet, det var bestemt til. Når et stykke tømmer var bestemt til bagbordssiden, på engelsk larboard,, blev det mærket sådan her — "L." Når et stykke var til styrbordssiden, starboard, blev det mærket sådan her — "S." Et stykke til bagbordssiden forude, forward, blev mærket sådan her — "L. F." Når et stykke var til styrbordssiden forude, blev det mærket sådan her — "S. F." Til bagbord agter, aft, blev det mærket sådan her — "L. A." Til styrbord agter blev det mærket sådan her — "S. A." Jeg lærte snart navnene på disse bogstaver og hvad de stod for, når de blev anbragt på et stykke tømmer på skibsværftet. Jeg begyndte straks at kopiere dem, og på kort tid var jeg i stand til at lave de fire nævnte bogstaver. Derefter, når jeg mødte en dreng, jeg vidste kunne skrive, sagde jeg til ham, at jeg kunne skrive lige så godt som han. Hans næste ord var: »Det tror jeg ikke på. Lad mig se dig prøve.« Så lavede jeg de bogstaver, jeg havde været heldig nok til at lære, og bad ham gøre det bedre. På den måde fik jeg en hel del lektioner i at skrive, som jeg sandsynligvis aldrig ville have fået på nogen anden måde. I denne tid var min skrivebog plankehegnet, murstensvæggen og fortovet; min pen og blæk var et stykke kridt. Med disse lærte jeg for det meste at skrive. Jeg begyndte derpå at kopiere de kursive bogstaver i Websters stavebog og blev ved, indtil jeg kunne lave dem alle uden at se i bogen. På dette tidspunkt var min lille herre Thomas begyndt i skole, havde lært at skrive og fyldt en del skrivebøger. Disse var blevet bragt hjem, vist til nogle af vores nære naboer og derefter lagt til side. Min husfrue plejede at gå til religiøst kredsmøde i forsamlingshuset på Wilk Street hver mandag eftermiddag og lade mig passe huset. Når jeg blev efterladt sådan, brugte jeg tiden på at skrive i de tomme felter i min herre Thomas' skrivebog og kopierede, hvad han havde skrevet. Jeg blev ved med det, indtil jeg kunne skrive en håndskrift, der lignede min herre Thomas' meget. Og således lykkedes det mig, efter en lang, møjsommelig anstrengelse gennem mange år, til sidst at lære at skrive.

adjustments.before: 7. Lad os vogte os mod at sætte triste ansigter op ved ordet »tortur« — der er bestemt i dette tilfælde nok at trække fra, nok at slå af — der er endda noget at le ad. For vi må bestemt ikke undervurdere den kendsgerning, at Schopenhauer, der i praksis behandlede seksualiteten som en personlig fjende (inklusive dens redskab, kvinden, denne »instrumentum diaboli«), havde brug for fjender for at holde sig i godt humør; at han elskede grumme, bitre, sortgrønne ord; at han rasede for at rase, af lidenskab; at han ville være blevet syg, ville være blevet pessimist (for han var ikke pessimist, hvor meget han end ønskede at være det), uden sine fjender, uden Hegel, kvinden, sanseligheden og hele viljen til at eksistere, til at blive her. Uden dem ville Schopenhauer ikke have »blevet ved«, det er et sikkert væddemål; han ville være løbet væk: men hans fjender holdt ham fast, hans fjender lokkede ham altid tilbage til tilværelsen, hans vrede var, ligesom hos de gamle kynikere, hans lindring, hans adspredelse, hans erstatning, hans middel mod væmmelse, hans lykke. Så meget med hensyn til, hvad der er mest personligt i tilfældet Schopenhauer; på den anden side er der stadig meget, som er typisk hos ham — og først nu vender vi tilbage til vores problem. Det er en accepteret og ubestridelig kendsgerning, så længe der er filosoffer i verden, og hvor end filosoffer har eksisteret (fra Indien til England, for at tage de modsatte poler af filosofisk dygtighed), at der eksisterer en virkelig irritation og et nag fra filosoffernes side over for sanseligheden. Schopenhauer er blot det mest veltalende, og hvis man har øre for det, også det mest fascinerende og fortryllende udbrud. Der eksisterer ligeledes en virkelig filosofisk forudindtagethed og forkærlighed for hele det asketiske ideal; der bør ikke være illusioner på dette punkt. Begge disse følelser, som er blevet sagt, hører til typen; hvis en filosof mangler dem begge, så er han — det kan I være sikre på — aldrig andet end en »pseudo«. Hvad betyder dette? For denne tilstand må først fortolkes: i sig selv står den der dum, til al evighed, som enhver »ting-i-sig-selv«. Hvert dyr, inklusive la bête philosophe, stræber instinktivt efter et optimum af gunstige betingelser, hvor det kan udfolde hele sin styrke og opnå den størst mulige følelse af magt; med samme instinkt og en fin sans, som overgår enhver fornuft, nærer hvert dyr en dødsangst for enhver forstyrrelse og hindring, der spærrer eller kunne spærre dets vej til dette optimum (jeg taler ikke om dets vej til lykke, men om dets vej til magt, til handling, den mægtigste handling, og faktisk i mange tilfælde om dets vej til ulykke). På samme måde nærer filosoffen en dødsangst for ægteskabet, sammen med alt, hvad der kunne overtale ham til det — ægteskabet som en fatal hindring på vejen til optimum. Hvilke store filosoffer har hidtil været gift? Heraklit, Platon, Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Kant, Schopenhauer — de var ikke gift, og endvidere kan man ikke forestille sig dem som gifte. En gift filosof hører til komedien, det er min regel; hvad angår undtagelsen Sokrates — den ondskabsfulde Sokrates giftede sig, tilsyneladende ironice, blot for at bevise netop denne regel. Hver filosof ville sige, som Buddha sagde, da fødslen af en søn blev meddelt ham: »Râhoula er født mig, en lænke er smedet for mig« (Râhoula betyder her »en lille dæmon«); der må komme en time af refleksion til hver »fri ånd« (forudsat at han tidligere har haft en time af tankeløshed), ligesom én engang kom til den samme Buddha: »Snævert indeklemt«, reflekterede han, »er livet i huset; det er et urent sted; friheden findes i at forlade huset.« Fordi han tænkte sådan, forlod han huset. Så mange broer til uafhængighed vises i det asketiske ideal, at filosoffen ikke kan undlade at fryde sig og klappe i hænderne, når han hører historien om alle disse beslutsomme mænd, der en dag ytrede et nej til al trældom og gik ud i en ørken; selv om vi indrømmer, at de blot var stærke æsler og den absolutte modsætning til stærke sind. Hvad betyder så det asketiske ideal hos en filosof? adjustments.before: 7. Let us beware of pulling dismal faces at the word "torture." In this case there is certainly plenty to deduct and plenty to discount; there is even something to laugh at. For we must not underestimate the fact that Schopenhauer treated sexuality in practice as a personal enemy (including its tool, woman, that "instrumentum diaboli"), and that he needed enemies to keep him in good humor. He loved grim, bitter, blackish-green words. He raged for the sake of raging, out of passion. Without his enemies, without Hegel, woman, sensuality and the whole "will for existence," "keeping on," he would have fallen ill and become a pessimist (for he was not a pessimist, however much he wished to be). Without them Schopenhauer would not have "kept on"; that is a safe wager. He would have run away. But his enemies held him fast, and his enemies always lured him back to existence. His wrath was, as it was for the ancient Cynics, his balm, his recreation, his recompense, his remedium against disgust, his happiness. So much for what is most personal in Schopenhauer's case. On the other hand, much in him is also typical, and only now do we come back to our problem. It is an accepted and indisputable fact that, as long as there have been philosophers in the world, and wherever they have existed (from India to England, to take the opposite poles of philosophic ability), they have felt a real irritation and rancor towards sensuality. Schopenhauer is merely its most eloquent outburst and, for anyone with an ear for it, also the most fascinating and enchanting. Philosophers likewise have a real bias and affection for the whole ascetic ideal; let there be no illusions on this score. Both feelings, as has been said, belong to the type. A philosopher who lacks both is, you may be certain, never anything but a "pseudo." What does this mean? For this state of affairs must first be interpreted: in itself it stands there stupid, for all eternity, like any "Thing-in-itself." Every animal, la bête philosophe included, strives instinctively for an optimum of favorable conditions, in which it can let its whole strength play and attain its maximum feeling of power. With equal instinctiveness, and with a fine perceptive flair superior to any reason, every animal shudders mortally at every kind of disturbance and hindrance that blocks, or could block, its way to that optimum. (I am not talking about his way to happiness, but about his way to power, to action, to the most powerful action, and in fact in many cases his way to unhappiness.) In the same way the philosopher shudders mortally at marriage and at all that could persuade him to it, since marriage is a fatal hindrance on the way to the optimum. Which great philosophers have been married, up to now? Heracleitus, Plato, Descartes, Spinoza, Leibnitz, Kant, Schopenhauer: none was married, and, what is more, one cannot imagine them married. A married philosopher belongs to comedy. That is my rule. As for the exception, Socrates, the malicious Socrates seems to have married ironice, just to prove this very rule. Every philosopher would say what Buddha said when the birth of a son was announced to him: "Râhoula has been born to me, a fetter has been forged for me" (Râhoula means here "a little demon"). An hour of reflection must come to every "free spirit" (granted that an hour of thoughtlessness came first), just as it once came to that same Buddha: "Narrowly cramped," he reflected, "is life in the house; it is a place of uncleanness; freedom is found in leaving the house." Thinking so, he left the house. The ascetic ideal shows so many bridges to independence that the philosopher cannot help exulting and clapping his hands when he hears the story of all those resolute men who one day said nay to all servitude and went into some desert, even granting that they were only strong asses and the absolute opposite of strong minds. What, then, does the ascetic ideal mean in a philosopher? This is my answer, which will have been guessed long ago: when he sees this ideal, the philosopher smiles, because he sees in it an optimum of the conditions for the highest and boldest intellectuality. He does not thereby deny "existence." Rather he affirms his existence, and only his existence, and this perhaps to the point of being not far from the blasphemous wish, pereat mundus, fiat philosophia, fiat philosophus, fiam!

adjustments.before: "The done and the undone," says the disciple of the Vedanta, "do him no harm; the good and the evil he shakes off, wise man that he is; his kingdom suffers no more from any act; good and evil, he goes beyond them both." — An entirely Indian conception, as Brahmanist as it is Buddhist. In neither the Indian nor the Christian doctrine is this "Redemption" thought to be reachable through virtue and moral improvement, however highly they rate the hypnotic efficiency of virtue. Keep clear on this point; it simply corresponds with the facts. That they stayed true on it is perhaps to be counted the best example of realism in the three great religions, which with this one exception are absolutely soaked in morality. "For those who know, there is no duty." "Redemption is not gained by acquiring virtues; for redemption consists in being one with Brahman, who cannot acquire any perfection; and it consists just as little in giving up faults, for the Brahman, unity with whom is what constitutes redemption, is eternally pure" (these passages are from the Commentaries of the Cankara, as quoted by the first real European expert on Indian philosophy, my friend Paul Deussen). So we wish to honor the idea of "redemption" in the great religions. But it is rather hard to stay serious when we see how highly these exhausted pessimists, too tired even to dream, esteem deep sleep — deep sleep taken, that is, as already a fusing into Brahman, as the attainment of the unio mystica with God. "When he has fallen completely asleep," says the oldest and most venerable "script" on this point, "and come to perfect rest, so that he sees no more any vision, then, oh dear one, he is united with Being, he has entered into his own self — encircled by the Self with its absolute knowledge, he has no more any consciousness of what is outside or of what is inside. Day and night do not cross these bridges, nor do age, death, suffering, good deeds or evil deeds." "In deep sleep," say likewise the believers in this deepest of the three great religions, "the soul lifts itself out of this body of ours, enters the supreme light and stands out in it in its true shape: there it is the supreme spirit itself, which travels about, jesting and playing and enjoying itself, whether with women, or chariots, or friends; there its thoughts turn no more back to this appanage of a body, to which the 'prana' (the vital breath) is harnessed like a beast of burden to the cart." None the less we will take care to realize (as we did when discussing "redemption") that, for all its pomp of Oriental extravagance, this simply expresses the same criticism of life as the clear, cold, Greekly cold, but still suffering Epicurus made. The hypnotic sensation of nothingness, the peace of deepest sleep, anæsthesia in short — that is what the sufferers and the utterly depressed take for their supreme good, their value of values, if you please; that is what must be treasured by them as something positive, and felt by them as the essence of the Positive (by the same logic of the feelings, nothingness is called God in all pessimistic religions).
